cards.claim: Learning rate decay and batch size increase are equivalent under SGD on noisy linear regression
cards.conditions: SGD on linear regression with additive noise, fixed learning rate and doubling batch size vs halving learning rate with fixed batch size, same number of samples processed per phase
cards.effect: Excess risk of batch-ramp process is within constant factor of learning-rate-decay process
cards.quote: Consider a base SGD process that runs for phases, using a fixed learning rate throughout, while the batch size doubles after each phase. Now consider an alternative process where the batch size is fixed but the learning rate halves after each phase, and where each phase processes the same number of data points as in the base process. Then, the excess risk of the base process is within a constant factor of that of the alternative process.

cards.claim: Normalized SGD (proxy for Adam) shows equivalence between learning rate decay and batch size ramp under variance-dominated regime
cards.conditions: Normalized SGD, batch size doubles and learning rate decays by factor √2, Assumption 2 holds (variance-dominated gradient norms), same samples per phase
cards.effect: Excess risk within constant factor when product αβ held constant
cards.quote: Consider a base normalized SGD process (Equation 4) that runs for phases, where the batch size doubles after each phase while the learning rate decays by a factor of √2. Consider an alternative normalized SGD process where the batch size is fixed but the learning rate halves after each phase, and where each phase processes the same number of data points as in the base process. Then, the excess risk of the base process is within a constant factor of that of the alternative process.

cards.claim: Seesaw scheduler maintains loss dynamics while reducing serial steps through coordinated batch size and learning rate adjustment
cards.conditions: When standard scheduler halves learning rate, multiply by √2 and double batch size
cards.effect: Preserves loss dynamics while reducing serial steps
cards.quote: whenever a standard scheduler would halve the learning rate, Seesaw instead multiplies it by √2 and doubles the batch size, preserving loss dynamics while reducing serial steps.

cards.claim: There exists a maximum aggressive batch ramp constraint at α·β ≤ 1/2
cards.conditions: At critical batch size, using Seesaw-style equivalence scheduling
cards.effect: More aggressive schedules (α·β > 1/2) diverge; less aggressive match baseline
cards.evidence: Theoretical constraint (Lemma 4) and empirical validation on 150M models
cards.quote: The most aggressive ramp up scheme we can use is given by α·β ≤ 1/2. (for a formal argument see Lemma 4)

cards.claim: Batch size ramping cannot match learning rate decay performance beyond critical batch size
cards.conditions: Batch sizes beyond CBS (tested at 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192 on 150M model), Adam/normalized SGD
cards.effect: Loss discrepancy increases with batch size beyond CBS; Seesaw underperforms cosine decay
cards.evidence: Empirical observation on multiple batch sizes (Figure 3) with theoretical explanation
cards.quote: past a certain batch size, it is not possible to match the performance of learning rate decay by any equivalent batch size ramp up for Adam or normalized SGD

cards.claim: Seesaw achieves approximately 28% wall-clock time reduction while maintaining validation loss at critical batch size
cards.conditions: 150M/300M/600M parameter models, Chinchilla scale, trained at critical batch size (CBS), equal FLOPs comparison
cards.effect: ~28% serial runtime reduction matching cosine decay loss dynamics
cards.evidence: Empirical results across three model scales (Figure 1, Table 1)
cards.quote: Empirically, on 150M/300M/600M-parameter models trained at Chinchilla scale using a constant (critical) batch size, Seesaw matches cosine decay at equal FLOPs while reducing wall-clock time by approximately 28%, approaching the theoretical limit implied by our analysis.

cards.claim: Seesaw works with practical Adam variant (AdamW) with tuned weight decay
cards.conditions: AdamW optimizer with weight decay tuning, LLM pretraining
cards.effect: Maintains performance and achieves wall-clock speedup
cards.quote: We also empirically show that Seesaw also works even when using AdamW with tuned weight decay in Figure 4 of Appendix C, making Seesaw a practical solution for reducing the wall-clock time of LLM pretraining.

cards.claim: Learning rate decay becomes necessary beyond critical batch size even with batch size increases due to NGD dynamics
cards.conditions: Batch sizes beyond CBS, gradient-dominated regime transitions to noise-dominated
cards.effect: Cannot reach minimizer with constant learning rate; cyclic convergence behavior prevents reaching optimum
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis with NGD toy example (1D quadratic loss), empirical support Figure 3
cards.quote: In order to escape this stable cycle and reach the minimizer, it is thus necessary to decay the learning rate. Therefore, if we slightly relax the setup and think of large batch training as being close to NGD regime, we can see that further increasing the batch size does not change the dynamics. Therefore, past a certain batch size, learning rate decay is crucial for achieving a lower loss with NGD.

cards.claim: Batch size ramping has been empirically used in practice but lacks theoretical justification
cards.conditions: Large-scale LLM pretraining (LLaMA, Nemotron, OLMo, Apertus)
cards.effect: Reduces training time without compromising performance in practice
cards.evidence: Empirical observations across multiple production LLM training runs (cited in literature)
cards.quote: recent large-scale LLM training runs employ batch size schedules that gradually increase batch size over the course of training (Dubey et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023; Adler et al., 2024; OLMo et al., 2024; Team, 2025). This practice has been observed to further reduce training times without compromising model performance. However, to the best of our knowledge, the "batch ramp" schedules are not theoretically grounded and instead tuned heuristically.

cards.claim: Assumption of variance-dominated gradient norms fails at large batch sizes, causing Seesaw equivalence to break down
cards.conditions: Batch size increases past CBS, normalized SGD/Adam, Assumption 2 no longer holds
cards.effect: Equivalence relationship collapses; bias term dominates over variance term in gradient denominator
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis with variance scaling (Equation 5) and empirical failure of Seesaw (Figure 3)
cards.quote: since the noise variance decreases with the batch size as O(1/B), one can see that past a certain batch the additive noise will become small, and thus Assumption 2 will fail.
